sections.b: Hebrews 11 begins with a description of faith, 'assurance about what is hoped for, and proof of realities no one can see' (Hebrews 11:1), and then shows it in people who acted on God's word before they saw the outcome: Noah building an ark, Abraham leaving home when 'he did not know where he was heading', Moses choosing 'the disgrace of the Messiah'. A middle section (Hebrews 11:13-16) says that all of them died without receiving what was promised and confessed that they were foreigners on the earth, looking for a heavenly country. The ending is the surprise: 'they would not be made perfect without us' (Hebrews 11:40). The heroes wait for the church, and in Hebrews 12:1 they surround it as a cloud of witnesses.

The roll call ends with deeds and sufferings rather than names: shutting lions' mouths (Daniel 6:22), putting out fire (Daniel 3), women receiving their dead (1 Kings 17:17-24; 2 Kings 4:18-37), the tortured who refused release to gain 'a better resurrection' (2 Maccabees 6-7), those stoned (2 Chronicles 24:21), sawn in two (Jewish tradition of Isaiah's death), killed by the sword (1 Kings 19:10; Jeremiah 26:23), and prophets wandering in sheepskins like Elijah. 'The world was not worth them' (Hebrews 11:38).

common: Most readers take Hebrews 11 as a sermon on the whole Old Testament read through the single theme of faith.
uncommon: Some read 'they would not be made perfect without us' (Hebrews 11:40) as meaning the Old Testament faithful entered God's full presence only after Christ's death.

claude.title: The roll call ends with the hearers (Claude's theory)
claude.body: This is Claude's reading. The chapter is built so that the last name on the list is missing: after the named heroes and the nameless martyrs, 'something better ... for us' (Hebrews 11:40) leaves a space for the congregation itself, who had already suffered insult, prison and loss (Hebrews 10:32-34). The 'so then, we too' of Hebrews 12:1 fills the space. The roll call is less a museum than an invitation to add one's own name by enduring.

sections.h: Faith in Hebrews: endurance toward what is promised
sections.b: Hebrews quotes Habakkuk 2:4 in the form 'my righteous one will live by faith. And if he shrinks back, my soul is not pleased with him' (Hebrews 10:38), and sets faith against shrinking back (Hebrews 10:39). Faith in Hebrews looks forward: it is 'assurance about what is hoped for' (Hebrews 11:1), it pleases God because it believes 'that he is, and that he pays back those who search hard for him' (Hebrews 11:6), and it shows itself in obedience and endurance. Jesus is 'the Founder and perfecter of faith' (Hebrews 12:2), the one who ran the whole course first.

sections.h: Hebrews: the new covenant and the end of offerings
sections.b: Hebrews quotes Jeremiah 31:31-34 in full (Hebrews 8:8-12) and again in part (Hebrews 10:16-17). It draws two conclusions. From the word 'new': God 'has made the first one old', and what is aging 'is close to disappearing' (Hebrews 8:13). From the last line: since God will 'never again remember their sins', 'there is no more offering for sin' (Hebrews 10:17-18). Jesus is 'mediator of a new covenant' (Hebrews 9:15; 12:24), and his blood is 'the blood of an eternal covenant' (Hebrews 13:20). The Greek text Hebrews quotes says God 'neglected' the ancestors who did not stay in the covenant (Hebrews 8:9), where the Hebrew says he had married them (Jeremiah 31:32).
sections.refs: Hebrews 8:6-13; Hebrews 9:15-22; Hebrews 10:15-18; Hebrews 12:24; Hebrews 13:20; Jeremiah 31:31-34

common: Christians read Hebrews 8 as the New Testament's fullest use of Jeremiah 31.
uncommon: Some Christian readers hold that Hebrews 8:13 speaks of the Sinai priesthood and sacrifices growing old, not of God's covenant with the Jewish people, and read it with Romans 11:29.

sections.b: The Greek diathēkē, the Septuagint's word for covenant, also meant a last will. Hebrews uses it seventeen times; in Hebrews 9:16-17 the argument turns on the second sense: 'in the case of a will, someone must bring proof that the one who made it has died'. The writer then returns to the covenant at Sinai, put in force with blood (Exodus 24:8; Hebrews 9:18-20). Readers differ on whether the writer plays on two senses of the word or keeps 'covenant' throughout, with the death of a sacrificed animal standing for the parties.

sections.h: The tent in Hebrews: copy and true
sections.b: Hebrews calls the tabernacle 'the tent' (skēnē) and reads it through Exodus 25:40: Moses built by 'the pattern you were shown on the mountain', so the earthly tent is 'a copy and a shadow of the things in heaven' (Hebrews 8:5). Christ serves in 'the true tent, which the Lord pitched' (Hebrews 8:2) and went 'through the greater and more perfect tent, not made by human hands' (Hebrews 9:11). Hebrews 9:1-5 lists the tent's two rooms and their furniture, placing a golden altar of incense with the most holy place, a famous difficulty beside Exodus 30:6. The patriarchs too lived 'in tents' (Hebrews 11:9), and 'the people who worship in the tent' have no right to eat from the Christian altar (Hebrews 13:10).
sections.refs: Hebrews 8:2-5; Hebrews 9:1-11, 21, 24; Hebrews 11:9; Hebrews 13:10; Exodus 25:40; Exodus 30:6

sections.h: Hebrews 9-10: the Day of Atonement fulfilled
sections.b: Hebrews reads Christ's death and ascension through Leviticus 16. Only the high priest entered the inner room, 'once a year, and never without blood' (Hebrews 9:7); Christ 'entered the sanctuary once for all ... through his own blood' (Hebrews 9:12), into 'heaven itself, to appear now before the face of God on our behalf' (Hebrews 9:24). The repetition every year showed the offerings could not take away sins (Hebrews 10:1-4). As the people waited for the high priest to come out, believers wait for Christ to 'be seen a second time' (Hebrews 9:28). The bodies of the sin offerings burned 'outside the camp' (Leviticus 16:27) become the picture of Jesus suffering 'outside the gate' (Hebrews 13:11-13).

Hebrews argues that animal sacrifices could not take away sins (Hebrews 10:4) and that God wanted obedience (Psalm 40:6-8, quoted in the Septuagint form 'a body you made ready for me', Hebrews 10:5). Christ offered 'one sacrifice for sins, good for all time' and took his seat (Hebrews 10:12); 'with one offering he has made perfect, for all time, the people who are being made holy' (Hebrews 10:14); so 'there is no more offering for sin' (Hebrews 10:18). Christians now offer 'a sacrifice of praise' and the sacrifices of kindness and sharing (Hebrews 13:15-16). The churches divide over how the Lord's Supper relates to this one sacrifice: see the card at Hebrews 10.

Hebrews contrasts the priests who 'stand' at their duties 'day after day' with Christ, who 'offered one sacrifice for sins ... and took his seat at God's right hand' (Hebrews 10:11-12). On earth he would not even be a priest, since he was not of Levi (Hebrews 8:4); he is 'a minister of the sanctuary and of the true tent' in heaven (Hebrews 8:2), 'a great priest over God's house' (Hebrews 10:21).

'By the law's rules, almost everything is made clean with blood. And no forgiveness comes about without blood being poured out' (Hebrews 9:22), a summary of Leviticus 17:11. Hebrews traces blood through the covenant at Sinai (Hebrews 9:18-21), the Day of Atonement (Hebrews 9:7, 12, 25), the Passover (Hebrews 11:28) and the 'blood of sprinkling, which speaks better than Abel' (Hebrews 12:24; Genesis 4:10). Christ's own blood opens the way into the sanctuary (Hebrews 10:19) and is 'the blood of an eternal covenant' (Hebrews 13:20).

sections.b: Hebrews has its own vocabulary for how the old order points to the new: the earthly sanctuary is 'a copy and a shadow' (Hebrews 8:5) of the heavenly one, built by the 'pattern' (typos) shown to Moses; the tent was 'a parable for the time now present' (Hebrews 9:9); the earthly sanctuary is a 'copy' (antitypa, Hebrews 9:24) of the true one; the law has 'a shadow of the good things to come, not the actual image' (Hebrews 10:1). Note that Hebrews uses antitypos for the copy, the opposite of the later Christian use of 'antitype' for the fulfillment.
sections.refs: Hebrews 8:5; Hebrews 9:9, 23-24; Hebrews 10:1; Exodus 25:40; Colossians 2:17; 1 Peter 3:21

sections.b: Hebrews 10:26-31 repeats the warning of Hebrews 6:4-8: 'if we keep on sinning by choice after we have come to know the truth fully, there is no longer any sacrifice for sins left'. It names the act as stamping on the Son of God and treating 'the blood of the covenant, the blood that made him holy' as common. Wesley's note reads this as total apostasy by one who had been justified; Calvin limits it to those who wholly forsake Christ and his church, and rejects its use to deny pardon to all who fall after baptism. Hebrews 12:16-17 adds Esau, who 'found no place for repentance'. The card on the question is at Hebrews 6:4-6.

sections.h: Hebrews: Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead
sections.b: Hebrews says Abraham offered Isaac 'when God put him to the test', though Isaac was the son of the promise (Genesis 21:12), because 'he reckoned that God could raise people even from the dead, and from there, in a kind of parable, he did get him back' (Hebrews 11:17-19). The reading draws on Abraham's words, 'We will worship, and then we will come back to you' (Genesis 22:5). James uses the same scene for faith shown in works (James 2:21-23).

Abraham fills the center of the roll call: he left home when 'he did not know where he was heading', lived 'as a resident alien in the promised land' in tents, waited for 'the city with foundations, the city whose architect and maker is God', received power with Sarah to father children past the age for it, and offered Isaac (Hebrews 11:8-19). Hebrews reads his whole life as looking toward a heavenly homeland (Hebrews 11:13-16).

Hebrews 11:11 is the same string of Greek letters in every edition, but the editions read it two ways. Most (Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, NA28, the Byzantine text) make Sarah the one whose faith 'received power to conceive', as the KJV and most Bibles do; NA28 adds 'barren', and the Byzantine text 'she gave birth'. The SBL edition, following the margin of Westcott-Hort, reads 'with Sarah herself' and makes Abraham the subject, because 'power for the laying down of seed' is a father's part; the Plain English Translation follows the SBL here. Either way Sarah stands in the roll call, and 1 Peter 3:6 also holds her up as a model.

Hebrews quotes Genesis 5:24 in the form found in Swete's Septuagint: Enoch 'was not found, because God had carried him off', and before that 'he had pleased God' (Hebrews 11:5). From 'pleased God' the writer concludes that Enoch had faith, since 'no one can please him at all' without faith (Hebrews 11:6). The Hebrew says Enoch 'walked with God'.

Hebrews says Abel offered 'a fuller sacrifice than Cain's' by faith, and 'through it he still speaks, though he died' (Hebrews 11:4). Later it says Jesus' blood 'speaks better than Abel' (Hebrews 12:24), recalling the blood that cried from the ground (Genesis 4:10).

Noah, 'given warning about things no one could see yet, acted out of reverence and built an ark so that his household would be saved'; by it 'he passed sentence on the world' and inherited 'the righteousness that matches faith' (Hebrews 11:7).

Hebrews tells Moses' story as a series of choices by faith: his parents hid him and did not fear the king's decree; grown up, he refused to be known as the son of Pharaoh's daughter and chose 'the disgrace of the Messiah' over Egypt's treasures; he left Egypt 'as if he could see the one who cannot be seen'; he kept the Passover (Hebrews 11:23-28). In Hebrews 12:21 Moses says at the mountain, 'I am full of terror', words drawn from Deuteronomy 9:19.

'By faith Rahab the prostitute was not destroyed along with the disobedient, since she had taken in the spies in peace' (Hebrews 11:31). James uses the same welcome to ask whether she was 'justified by works' (James 2:25). She is one of the few women named in the roll call.

The last part of the roll call names no one but describes the tortured who refused release 'so that they could win a better resurrection' (2 Maccabees 6-7), those stoned, sawn in two (the tradition of Isaiah's death under Manasseh, told in the Martyrdom of Isaiah and the Babylonian Talmud), and killed with the sword. In Hebrews 12:1 the faithful become 'a cloud of witnesses' (martyres), and Hebrews 12:4 tells the readers they have not yet resisted 'to the point of blood'.

Without naming it, Hebrews 12:18-21 describes Sinai from Exodus 19-20 and Deuteronomy 4-5: a mountain that could be touched, fire, darkness, gloom, whirlwind, trumpet, and a voice so terrifying that the hearers begged that no more be spoken. Even an animal that touched the mountain was to be stoned. Hebrews sets it against Mount Zion, to which believers 'have come near'.

'But you have come near to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, heavenly Jerusalem' (Hebrews 12:22): angels in festival, the assembly of the firstborn, God the judge of all, the spirits of the righteous made perfect, Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and the sprinkled blood. The writer speaks of worship now, not only of the future.

Hebrews traces the city from Abraham, who waited for 'the city with foundations, the city whose architect and maker is God' (Hebrews 11:10), through the patriarchs, for whom God 'has a city ready' (Hebrews 11:16), to the readers, who have come near to 'heavenly Jerusalem' (Hebrews 12:22) and yet 'do not have a city here that remains' and search 'for the one that is coming' (Hebrews 13:14).

Hebrews 12:26-27 quotes Haggai 2:6 in a Greek form, 'Once more I will shake not only the earth but heaven too', and reads 'once more' as a final shaking in which the shaken things, 'things that were made', are moved away, so that the unshakable remains. The readers are 'receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken' (Hebrews 12:28).

Hebrews lists the ark of the covenant, 'covered with gold all around', with a golden jar of manna, Aaron's budded staff and the tablets of the covenant inside it, and the cherubim of glory overshadowing the atonement lid (Hebrews 9:4-5). Exodus places the manna and the staff 'in front of' the testimony, and 1 Kings 8:9 says only the tablets were inside by Solomon's day. The Greek word for the lid, hilastērion, is the one Paul uses in Romans 3:25.

sections.b: Hebrews sets 'a heifer's ashes sprinkled on people who have become unclean' beside the blood of goats and bulls: such rites made the flesh clean, so 'how much more will the blood of Christ ... clean our conscience' (Hebrews 9:13-14).

'Do not forget to welcome strangers, for by this some people have had angels as guests without knowing it' (Hebrews 13:2), recalling Abraham (Genesis 18), Lot (Genesis 19), Manoah (Judges 13) and, for Catholic and Orthodox readers, Tobias and Raphael (Tobit 5).

Hebrews warns against being like Esau, who sold his birthright for one meal (Hebrews 12:16), and then tells the readers they have come near to 'the assembly of the firstborn whose names are listed in the heavens' (Hebrews 12:23). Israel was God's firstborn (Exodus 4:22); the church shares that standing and must not trade it away.

Hebrews 12:16-17 calls Esau one who 'treats holy things as nothing' and says he 'found no place for repentance, though he searched for it with tears' (Genesis 27:34-38). Jewish tradition also judged Esau harshly: the Babylonian Talmud lists five sins he committed on the day he sold the birthright (Bava Batra 16b).

sections.h: The spirits of the righteous made perfect
sections.b: Hebrews 12:23 speaks of 'the spirits of righteous people who have been made perfect', present in the heavenly city to which the worshiping church has come near. Hebrews 11:40 says the faithful of old 'would not be made perfect without us'. Hebrews 9:27 sets death and judgment in order: 'it is in store for human beings to die once, and after this, judgment'.

Hebrews 13:10 says 'We have an altar, and the people who worship in the tent have no right to eat from it.' It is read of the cross, of Christ himself (Calvin: 'the word altar includes sacrificing and the victim'), or of the Eucharistic table. Hebrews 9:20 also gives Moses' words in the form 'This is the blood of the covenant', close to Jesus' words over the cup (Mark 14:24).

Hebrews closes: 'Know that our brother Timothy has been released. If he comes soon enough, I will bring him along when I see you' (Hebrews 13:23). No other text mentions this imprisonment. The note places the unnamed writer within Paul's circle.

Hebrews 13:24 sends greetings from 'the people from Italy'. Many read this as Italians away from home greeting the church in Rome, which would make Rome the letter's destination; others read it as Christians in Italy greeting a church elsewhere. Acts 18:2 tells of Aquila and Priscilla, who 'had just come from Italy' after Claudius ordered the Jews out of Rome.

sections.h: Chapters 8-13: the argument's center and the call to endure
sections.b: Hebrews 8-10 is the center of the sermon: Christ the high priest of a better covenant (Jeremiah 31), the earthly tent and the Day of Atonement, Christ entering heaven with his own blood, one sacrifice once for all (Psalm 40), and the call to come near. Then the second warning (Hebrews 10:26-31), the roll call of faith (Hebrews 11), the race and the discipline of sons, Sinai and Zion (Hebrews 12), and the practical close 'outside the camp' (Hebrews 13). The writer calls the whole a 'word of exhortation' (Hebrews 13:22), the phrase used for a synagogue sermon in Acts 13:15.
